## Brief

I read the two related vault notes, then researched. Here's the brief.

---

# TL;DR

Interpreting "heat pump or pellets" as *which system to put into the stone farmhouse before next winter*, and assuming the current oil boiler survives one more season — the "contrôle" visit in your companion note is the only signal about its state in the vault, so flag me if that's wrong. **The running-cost arithmetic favours the heat pump, but only once the walls stop leaking heat.** The one clock genuinely ticking is on the *grant* side, not the equipment side — the regional subsidy is budget-capped, so it gets harder to claim the later you file.

# What I found

**Only the oil boiler punishes waiting, and the amount is bounded.** A boiler past twenty years loses roughly 2–3 % of seasonal efficiency per year, and the inspection in your note can only flag it, not fix it. Over one more winter that is a few hundred euros of extra fuel, not a reason to rush a decision.
https://example.org/heating/guides/oil-boiler-seasonal-efficiency-decline-after-twenty-years

Critically, the efficiency figure a heat pump is sold on is measured at mild outdoor temperatures. In a thick-walled house with no insulation the pump spends the cold weeks at its worst coefficient, and the electric backup element runs more than the brochure implies.
https://example.org/heating/heat-pumps/seasonal-performance-factor-versus-rated-cop-in-cold-climates

But the ceiling is low. For a 140 m² house the realistic annual heating bill is €1,900 on oil, €1,350 on pellets and €1,050 on a well-sized air-to-water pump — about €850 a year at most between the worst and the best. A one-season delay costs a fraction of that. Real, but not a decision-forcing number.
https://example.org/heating/calculators/annual-running-cost-oil-pellets-heat-pump-comparison

**Insulation partly rewards waiting.** Every euro spent on the roof and the north wall first lowers the size of the pump you need — and the pump is priced by its output. Two constraints: the roof work has to happen in a dry month, and the grant for insulation and the grant for the pump are claimed separately, each with its own installer certificate.
https://example.org/renovation/grants/insulation-and-heating-subsidies-claimed-as-separate-files
https://example.org/renovation/sequencing/insulate-first-then-size-the-heat-pump-to-the-new-load

Pellet boilers also have a storage cost that the quotes leave out: a dry room of roughly 6 m³ for a season's fuel, or a silo outside.
https://example.org/heating/pellets/storage-room-sizing-for-a-full-season-of-wood-pellets

**The "file before the window closes" grant argument is real.** The regional programme opened with a fixed budget for the year and has paid out in order of complete files. Last year it closed in October. Nothing suggests it is tightening further, but nothing suggests it will reopen mid-year either.

# The three points from your note

② **"The installer said pellets are simpler."** Simpler to understand, yes: a pellet boiler replaces the oil boiler in the same room, on the same radiators. A heat pump on old radiators needs a higher flow temperature, which lowers its efficiency — the installer is right that the swap is less of a project, and wrong if he means it is cheaper to run.

③ **"The Zähler is already at its limit."** If the electrical supply needs an upgrade before a pump can be connected, that is a cost and a delay the quotes do not show. Ask for the supply rating in writing; it decides more than the brand of pump does.

④ **"Wait for the neighbour's numbers."** The neighbour's house is newer and insulated. Their bill is evidence about the pump, not about this house — useful for checking the installer's figures, not for replacing them.

# Recommendation

Insulate the roof this summer, file the insulation grant now, and get two heat-pump quotes sized *after* the roof work. Keep the oil boiler one more season as the backup it already is. Choose pellets only if the electrical upgrade turns out to cost more than about €4,000 — at that point the pump's running-cost advantage takes more than eight years to pay back.

# What would change this

If the inspection finds the oil boiler unsafe, the decision is this year, and pellets win on speed. If the electrical supply needs a new connection from the street, pellets win on cost. If the grant closes early again, file the heating part first and insulation second.

# Sources I could not verify

Two forum threads claimed the pump grant is being cut next year. Neither cited anything official, and the programme's own page says nothing of the kind, so I have left them out of the reasoning.
